Motivation. The force that initiates, directs, and sustains behavior toward achieving goals or satisfying needs. Psychologists conceptualize it as the internal or external drivers that compel action, ranging from biological drives like hunger to psychological goals like achievement and belonging. Understanding motivation has become central to psychology, education, and organizational behavior, with major theories explaining everything from survival-level needs to self-fulfillment.

Biological drives represent the most fundamental motivators. Hunger, thirst, sexual reproduction—shared across species. These drive-reduction mechanisms were central to early behavioral psychology. Abraham Maslow theorized a hierarchy of needs, proposing that lower needs like physiological and safety needs must be satisfied before higher psychological needs—belonging, esteem, self-actualization—become motivating forces.

Extrinsic motivation, driven by external rewards or punishments, can be more immediate and effective for simple tasks but often proves less sustainable than intrinsic motivation. Intrinsic motivation comes from inherent satisfaction, autonomy, mastery, and purpose.

Martin Seligman's concept of learned helplessness revealed something crucial. Repeated uncontrollable failure can eliminate motivation, demonstrating the psychological basis of depression and apathy even when escape becomes possible. Herzberg's two-factor theory separates motivators like achievement, recognition, and responsibility from hygiene factors like salary, security, and working conditions, arguing the two operate independently and both matter.

Goal-setting theory emphasizes that clear, specific, challenging objectives generate stronger motivation than vague aspirations, but only when feedback and commitment are present. Cultural variation exists in what motivates individuals. Individualistic societies emphasize personal achievement and autonomy, while collectivist societies emphasize group harmony and relational obligations.

Self-determination theory emphasizes three core needs. Autonomy, competence, and relatedness. Intrinsic motivation flourishes when all three are satisfied. These various theories relate closely to Abraham Maslow and his hierarchy of needs, which remains the most influential framework for understanding human motivation.
